title: Messy Markbooks: Monitoring Participation in (and Across) Lessons
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau describes adopting a simple clipboard-based seating-plan tracker after years of using mini-whiteboards to monitor attention and understanding, crediting a Doug Lemov conference clip of a teacher tracking student responses on a clipboard as the spark. His own system is minimal: a hand-drawn seating plan with names, ticks for answered questions, dots for "I don't know" responses (a flag to return to that student later), circles for absences, and stars for praise-worthy moments. He contrasts this with colleague Claire Woozley's more elaborate "messy markbook" approach, which layers pastoral information - reading ages, SEND status - directly onto the seating plan alongside lesson notes and a monitoring route around the room, creating a running record teachers can consult over time to compare participation and identify who has and hasn't been heard from. Didau frames the whole post modestly, describing the tool as neither original nor sophisticated but genuinely useful, particularly for teachers like him who often teach classes of students they don't know well and need an externalised way to hold classroom information that would otherwise depend on memory. A footnote credits the messy markbook concept's origin to Christine Counsell.
points: Didau's clipboard system began as a memory aid borrowed from watching Doug Lemov's conference footage of a teacher tracking who'd been asked questions, adapted into a running seating-plan tally of ticks, dots, and stars.

His colleague Claire Woozley's more elaborate messy markbook version layers in pastoral data (reading ages, SEND status) alongside lesson notes, turning the same basic tool into a longitudinal record of both participation and prior knowledge.
The dot-for-"I don't know" convention is a small but deliberate accountability mechanism: it flags students to return to later in the same lesson rather than letting a non-answer pass unaddressed.

Didau credits the technique (originally, he notes, devised by Christine Counsell) with closing a real gap for teachers who don't know their students well, since it externalises memory that would otherwise depend on knowing each child.
quotes: Since taking the plunge with mini-whiteboards (see this post) over the past few years my ability to know whether students are paying attention, thinking and practising has dramatically increased.

One clip that stuck in my mind was of a teacher using a clipboard to help him remember what students had said, whether they'd been asked questions and anything else that might, in the hurly burly of the classroom, be forgotten.
I write down names because I don't know the children and tick them when they have answered a question. I make a dot where a students has said, "I don't know," to make sure I go back to them.
The arrows show her intended plan around the room when monitoring students' activity and the ticks indicate where students have answered questions.

Because they contain much more information, she can refer back to them over time to quickly check what has been taught, she can compare students' performance over time and see who's contributed to lessons in particularly helpful ways

So, that's it: one simple, straightforward way to make yourself more efficient in the classroom. I don't want to claim this is anything especially original but I've found the combination of seating plans plus a clipboard to be a revelation.
